metadata.title: Towards the implementation of automated scoring in international large-scale assessments: Scalability and quality control

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2023 constructed-response item responses (dichotomously scored 0/1) to train and test automated scoring models, with an 80:20 split across countries. The paper does not report applying TIMSS complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or any replicate-weight variance estimation; instead, it evaluates agreement and distributional differences between human and machine scores on a held-out test set. Because the task is supervised classification of item-level correctness using scikit-learn neural networks and LLM-based translation/scoring, the manuscript does not describe weight-aware estimation. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as model performance on the sampled item responses rather than as population-representative estimates of achievement.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are item-level dichotomous correctness labels (0/1) derived from human scoring of three TIMSS constructed-response items, not PV-based achievement scales. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper’s main exclusions are rule-based (e.g., aberrant responses and untranslatable/uncertain translations removed from training/test sets) rather than a documented statistical missing-data procedure (e.g., imputation or explicit missingness model). This means transparency about how any remaining missingness was treated is limited.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2023 constructed-response science items: Item 1 (Grade 4 Physical Science), Item 2 (Grade 4 Life Science), and Item 3 (Grade 8 Physics). Responses were dichotomously scored (1=correct, 0=incorrect) using human scores as training targets. Aberrant responses consisting solely of punctuation, numbers, single characters, or repetitive characters were automatically assigned machine score 0 and excluded from the automated scoring training/validation process. Untranslated responses were identified (for Google Translate) and removed; for ChatGPT translation, responses labeled "uncertain" were re-translated and those still "uncertain" were removed. The remaining dataset was split into training and test sets using an 80:20 ratio across all countries. For the MMT_ANN approach, the final MT engine per language group was selected using training-set human-machine agreement, and then individual-response-level translation adjustments were applied; responses that could not be translated by either method were filtered out.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2023 Grade 4 Physical Science (Item 1, constructed response)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Supervised ANN scoring (MMT_ANN) — Exact agreement (EA): 92.49%, Cohen’s kappa: 0.83; mean standardized mean score difference (SMD): 0.02 (human vs machine means). Best among compared methods (MMT_ANN vs Google_ANNs, ChatGPT_ANNs, Unsupervised Learning).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 4 Physical Science Item 1 the study leveraged machine translation method and response language group (with controls reflecting human scoring inconsistency and translation error type) to predict item-response correctness, finding that the mixed Google+ChatGPT ANN (MMT_ANN) achieved the highest human-machine agreement (EA=92.49%, κ=0.83) with near-zero mean score bias (SMD=0.02). This indicates that multilingual automated scoring for short constructed responses can be implemented at scale as a quality-control layer, provided translation quality is monitored and language-specific misalignment is investigated.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2023 Grade 4 Life Science (Item 2, constructed response)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Supervised ANN scoring (MMT_ANN) — EA: 94.19%, Cohen’s kappa: 0.87; SMD: −0.02 (human vs machine means). Best among compared methods (MMT_ANN vs Google_ANNs, ChatGPT_ANNs, Unsupervised Learning).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 4 Life Science Item 2 the study leveraged machine translation method and response language group (alongside human scoring inconsistency and translation error type) to predict item-response correctness, finding that MMT_ANN produced the strongest agreement with human scoring (EA=94.19%, κ=0.87) and minimal distributional shift (SMD=−0.02). This indicates that combining multiple MT engines with an ANN classifier can deliver consistent multilingual scoring performance, supporting operational adoption of automated scoring for CR items while still requiring targeted review for low-agreement country-language groups.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Supervised ANN scoring (MMT_ANN) — EA: 94.88%, Cohen’s kappa: 0.87; SMD: −0.01 (human vs machine means). Best among compared methods (MMT_ANN vs Google_ANNs, ChatGPT_ANNs, Unsupervised Learning).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2023 Grade 8 Physics Item 3 the study leveraged machine translation method and response language group (with attention to human scoring inconsistency and translation error type) to predict item-response correctness, finding that MMT_ANN achieved the highest agreement with human raters (EA=94.88%, κ=0.87) and essentially no mean-score bias (SMD=−0.01). This indicates that multilingual automated scoring can closely replicate human classifications for CR items, enabling scalable quality control in ILSAs while highlighting that misalignment (e.g., misspellings, low-resource languages, hallucinations) must be monitored rather than assumed away.

data.outcome_summary: The study evaluates automated scoring for three TIMSS 2023 science constructed-response items (Grade 4 Physical Science, Grade 4 Life Science, and Grade 8 Physics) using multilingual student responses across 42 languages (Items 1–2) and 40 countries (Item 3). Responses were dichotomously scored (0/1) by human raters and used to train feed-forward neural networks on bag-of-words features derived from translated/native English responses. Four scoring approaches were compared on an 80/20 train/test split: Google_ANNs, ChatGPT_ANNs, MMT_ANNs (mixed MT with response-level adjustments), and an unsupervised LLM-based majority/fuzzy matching approach. Across items, MMT_ANNs achieved the best agreement with human scoring (average EA=93.85%, κ=0.86) and the smallest mean-score differences (average SMD≈0). The paper reports misalignment averaging ~6% of responses, driven by human subjectivity/inconsistency and translation issues (misspellings, low-resource languages, polysemy, and occasional ChatGPT hallucinations). Limitations include reliance on bag-of-words (ignoring word order/context) and lack of documented survey-weight or missing-data handling procedures.
